ec559901b032b128.question: What does the customer want, and has the bank promised anything so far?

answer.answer: The customer wants her money back: the £650 deposit she paid by bank transfer on 27/10 for a used car, after the seller blocked her. The file does not show that the bank has promised her anything. There is no record of a refund or reimbursement being offered or promised. This looks like an authorised push payment scam, so under FRD-5 handlers must not promise reimbursement before the specialist decides, and under FRD-2 reimbursement is assessed by Fraud & Scams. The file also does not record any account protection steps or a handover.

9a4295d55d312ab3.question: What happened, in date order, and what is still unknown?

answer.answer: Timeline: On 27/10 the customer paid a £650 deposit by bank transfer for a used car seen on an online marketplace. The seller had sent photos and a fake logbook over WhatsApp, then blocked her after payment. She reported it on 30/10 and the complaint was received that day. She did not share bank security details. WhatsApp screenshots were emailed in. Not in the file: the time of the payment, the payee details (name, account), which account she paid from, whether the account was secured (FRD-4), and whether the case has been handed to Fraud & Scams. FRD-2 requires that handover within 1 business day. Her contact preference is also not recorded.

e39c4fba04278935.question: Which policy rules decide this case, and what do they require the handler to do?

answer.answer: This looks like an authorised push payment scam: the customer paid a £650 deposit by bank transfer, then the seller blocked her. Under FRD-2 and ESC-1 the case must go to Fraud & Scams within 1 business day (ESC-2). FRD-3 sets out the evidence the handover needs. FRD-4 requires the handler to check that the account is secured and record it. FRD-5 says no reimbursement may be promised. CH-6 treats a suspected scam as High severity, and ESC-3 lists the ten handover fields. Some details are not in the file: the time of the payment, the payee details, and any account-protection steps taken. The specialist decides any reimbursement, not the handler.

Where a customer was tricked into sending a payment to a fraudster, the case must be handed to the Fraud & Scams team within 1 business day. Reimbursement is assessed by a specialist, not by the complaints handler.
Suspected fraud, unauthorised transaction or scam → *Fraud & Scams*.
Handovers must be made within 2 business days of the trigger being identified (1 business day for scams, see FRD-2).

A fraud or scam handover must include: the date, time and amount of each disputed payment; the payee details as known; how the customer was contacted by the fraudster (if a scam); whether the customer shared any security details; and the date the customer reported it.
